title: Market Health: is the whole market moving, or just a few giants?
excerpt:
When the news says the market is up, it almost always means the S&P 500. But the S&P 500 is weighted by size, so a handful of giant companies can lift it while most stocks go nowhere, or fall.

Breadth asks a simpler question: out of every 100 stocks, how many are in an uptrend?

Think of a class of 100 students. If the class average rises because five top students scored higher, the class did not really improve. If 70 students improved, it did. The index is the class average. Breadth is the head count.

How to read the number
Above about 55: most stocks are taking part. A broad market.
Between 35 and 55: mixed.
Below about 35: most stocks are not taking part. A washed out market.

Where it stands. At the close on November 20, 43 of every 100 stocks we track were in an uptrend. Four weeks earlier it was 52.

The page shows the reading for all the stocks we track, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100, a chart back to 2021, and a row for each sector. Updated every evening. Open to everyone.

Market Health describes the market as it is today. It is not a forecast, and it is not a signal for any single stock.

Above about 55: most stocks are taking part. A broad market.

Where it stands. At the close on November 20, 43 of every 100 stocks we track were in an uptrend. Four weeks earlier it was 52.

What the page shows. The same reading for all the stocks we track, for the S&P 500 and for the Nasdaq-100. A chart of breadth against the index back to 2021, so you can see when the index rose on fewer and fewer stocks. And a row for each sector, so you can see where the strength and the weakness are.

It is updated every evening after the market closes, and it is open to everyone. No sign-in needed.

One caution. Market Health describes the market as it is today. It is not a forecast, and it is not a signal for any single stock.
